title: Checkpoint: Pharaohs and Power
objective: After this level you can explain how pharaohs, officials and ma'at held Egypt together.
summary: Ma’at gave the king his job; regalia announced it, viziers and scribes ran it, grain taxes paid for it and the army defended it, with royal women beside and sometimes on the throne.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: how one king held a whole country together.
cards.body: You’ve met the god-king, his props, his officials, his tax collectors, his army and the women around him. Here’s how the pieces fit.

events.label: Old Kingdom: the king tours the land to collect taxes
Middle Kingdom: Sobekneferu rules as king
New Kingdom: two viziers, and per-aa comes to mean the king

cards.headline: One system
cards.body: The king’s job was ma’at: setting order in place of isfet, chaos. The crook said he was his people’s herdsman. Administration and law both depended on him, but the vizier and a small class of scribes ran them, in a country where about 99 percent couldn’t read. Taxes came in as grain, and the state stored and redistributed it. Royal women stood beside the throne, and Sobekneferu and Hatshepsut sat on it. Order, paid for in wheat.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: The king’s job: ma’at, order in place of chaos
Regalia showed the office; viziers and scribes ran it
Grain taxes paid for it; the army defended it
Royal women stood beside the throne, and sometimes on it

questions.prompt: Pharaohs and Power recap: which royal symbol began as a herdsman’s staff?

options.label: The flail
The uraeus
options.rationale: That was the cobra on the forehead.

options.label: The nemes
The crook

questions.explanation: The crook stood for the king as herdsman of his people.

questions.prompt: Pharaohs and Power recap: how were viziers organized in the New Kingdom?

options.label: One vizier for each of the Two Lands
A single vizier for all of Egypt
One vizier in every province
No viziers: the king ran everything himself
options.rationale: The vizier was his chief deputy.

questions.explanation: By the New Kingdom there were two: one for Upper Egypt at Thebes and one for Lower Egypt at Memphis.

questions.prompt: Pharaohs and Power recap: how did Egypt’s government pay its way without money?

options.label: By borrowing coins from Rome
options.rationale: Coins arrived only much later, with foreign powers.

options.label: By collecting, storing and handing out goods like grain
By selling temples to foreign kings
It didn’t: nobody worked for the state
options.rationale: Egyptians could be called up to work for it.

questions.explanation: The nonmonetary economy ran on taxes in goods, stored in granaries and redistributed by the state.

questions.prompt: Pharaohs and Power recap: why did Egyptians treat keeping order as the king’s business?

options.label: The king was the only person who could read
Order was a tax the king collected
options.rationale: Ma’at was a duty, not a tax.

options.label: His role was to uphold ma’at and keep isfet at bay
The army refused to take orders from anyone else
options.rationale: The point was religious and cosmic.

questions.explanation: Ma’at was reaffirmed with each new king, and his duty was to set order in place of chaos.

questions.prompt: Pharaohs and Power recap: which of these came first?

options.label: Hatshepsut rules as king
options.rationale: She came in the New Kingdom.

options.label: Sobekneferu rules as king
Horse and chariot transform Egyptian warfare
options.rationale: That was the Second Intermediate Period.

options.label: Per-aa comes to mean the king himself
options.rationale: That began in the New Kingdom.

questions.explanation: Sobekneferu ruled at the end of the Middle Kingdom, before chariots arrived and long before Hatshepsut.
